courses.title: Special moves: castling, en passant and promotion
courses.desc: The three special rules that surprise every new player, each practised on the board.

lessons.text: Castling is the only move where two pieces move at once. The king slides two squares towards a rook, and the rook jumps over to stand beside it. It tucks your king into safety and brings a rook into the game.

move.prompt: Castle on the kingside: move your king two squares to the right.
move.done: Castled! Your king is safe behind three pawns and the rook is ready to join the game.

lessons.text: You may castle only if the king and that rook have never moved, the squares between them are empty, and the king is not in check, does not pass through an attacked square and does not land on one.

quiz.q: The black bishop on b4 is giving check. Can White castle right now?
options: No. You can never castle out of check
quiz.why: A king in check cannot castle. White must deal with the check first (for example with c3), and may castle later.

lessons.text: Black has just pushed a pawn two squares from d7 to d5, landing right beside your pawn. For one move only, you may capture it as if it had moved a single square. This is called en passant, French for 'in passing'.

move.prompt: Capture en passant: take your e-pawn diagonally to d6.
move.done: That's en passant. Your pawn lands on d6 and the black pawn on d5 disappears. Remember, the chance lasts for one move only.

lessons.text: A pawn that reaches the far end of the board must turn into a queen, rook, bishop or knight. Nearly always you choose a queen, the strongest piece. You can have more than one queen!

move.prompt: Push the pawn to the last rank.
move.done: A new queen. This is why an extra pawn in the endgame is often enough to win the game.

lessons.text: If the player to move has no legal move and is NOT in check, the game is a draw by stalemate. When you are far ahead, always leave the enemy king a move, or give check.

quiz.q: It is Black's move here. Black's king is not in check. What is the result?
quiz.why: The king on a8 has no safe square (a7, b7 and b8 are all covered) and Black has nothing else to move. That is stalemate: a draw. One move earlier, White should have left the king a square.

courses.title: Opening principles
courses.desc: Four rules that give you a good position in any opening: centre, development, king safety, and no wasted moves.

lessons.text: The four squares in the middle of the board are the most important. Pieces placed there reach the whole board, so both sides fight for them from move one. Start by putting a pawn in the centre.

move.prompt: Play a pawn two squares into the centre.
move.done: A centre pawn controls key squares and opens lines for your bishop and queen.

lessons.text: Development means bringing your knights and bishops off the back rank to useful squares. Knights usually come out first, towards the centre. The best developing moves also do something: attack a pawn, or defend one.

move.prompt: Develop a knight so that it attacks the pawn on e5.
move.done: Nf3 develops a piece, attacks e5 and gets you one step closer to castling.

lessons.t: Don't bring the queen out early
lessons.text: White has played 2.Qh5. It looks scary, but the queen is the easiest piece to chase. Black will defend calmly and then develop with gain of time by attacking her.

quiz.q: After 2...Nc6 3.Bc4 g6 4.Qf3 Nf6, who has more knights and bishops in play?
quiz.why: Black has two knights out and is ready to develop the bishop to g7; White has only a bishop out and has spent two moves on the queen. Every time you attack the queen with a developing move, you gain a move for free.

lessons.text: In the opening the centre often opens up, and a king stuck in the middle becomes a target. Castling moves it to the side behind a wall of pawns. Aim to castle within your first ten moves.

move.prompt: Your knight and bishop are out. Castle now.
move.done: King safe, rook active. Now you can play in the centre without worrying.

lessons.t: Rule 4: don't move the same piece twice
lessons.text: Each move in the opening should bring a new piece into play. Moving one piece again and again, or making lots of pawn moves on the edge, lets your opponent get ahead.

quiz.q: Which move for Black follows the opening principles best?
options: 3...h6, a pawn move on the edge
quiz.why: 3...Nf6 develops a new piece, attacks e4 and prepares castling. The other two moves develop nothing.

lessons.text: Development is finished when your knights and bishops are out, your king is castled and your queen has stepped off the back rank. Then nothing stands between your rooks: they are 'connected' and can move to the central files.

quiz.q: In this position, which side has finished development?
quiz.why: Both sides have all four minor pieces out, have castled and have moved the queen up one square. The rooks see each other. Now the middlegame begins.

courses.title: Checks, captures and threats
courses.desc: The simple routine strong players run on every move, so they stop missing tactics and stop giving pieces away.

lessons.text: Most moves can be ignored. Forcing moves cannot: a check must be answered, a capture usually has to be taken back, and a threat has to be stopped. So before every move, look at the forcing moves first, for you and for your opponent.

quiz.q: In which order should you look?
quiz.why: Checks first because they force the most; then captures; then threats. We call it CCT.

lessons.text: Start with checks. Look at every check, even ones that seem silly, because a check can be checkmate. Here the black king is boxed in by its own pawns.

move.prompt: Find the check that ends the game.
move.done: Checkmate on the back rank. The king's own pawns took away every escape square.

lessons.text: A check that also attacks a second piece wins that piece, because your opponent has to spend the move saving the king.

move.prompt: Find the check that also attacks the rook.
move.done: The queen checked the king and attacked the rook at the same time. That double attack is called a fork.

lessons.text: Next, look at every capture. Ask: is the piece defended? If nothing can take back, it is free. Start with captures of the most valuable pieces.

move.prompt: One black piece is undefended. Take it.
move.done: The queen was attacked by your knight and defended by nothing. Looking at every capture finds gifts like this.

lessons.text: A threat is a move that wins something next turn if your opponent ignores it. One threat can usually be stopped. Two threats at once often cannot.

move.prompt: Find the pawn move that attacks two pieces at once.
move.done: A pawn fork. Whichever piece moves away, the pawn takes the other one.

lessons.text: The routine works both ways. Before you choose your move, ask what your opponent's checks, captures and threats are. Here White's queen and bishop both aim at f7: the threat is Qxf7 checkmate.

move.prompt: You are Black. Stop the mate on f7.
move.done: The threat is stopped. Because you looked for White's forcing moves, the four-move checkmate failed, and now White's queen will lose time.

lessons.text: CCT takes a few seconds once it is a habit. Run it twice on every move: once for your opponent ('what does their last move threaten?') and once for yourself ('do I have a forcing move that wins?').

quiz.q: When should you run the CCT check?
options: On every move, for both sides
quiz.why: On every move, for both sides. Most games below master level are decided by a forcing move that one player did not look at. Practise it in the Tactics trainer until it is automatic.

courses.title: Is it safe? The blunder check
courses.desc: Count attackers and defenders, know what each piece is worth, and check your move before you play it.

lessons.text: To know whether a trade is good, give each piece a value: pawn 1, knight 3, bishop 3, rook 5, queen 9. The king has no value because it can never be traded.

quiz.q: You give up a knight and win a rook. How did the trade go?
quiz.why: A rook (5) for a knight (3) wins 2 points. Players call that 'winning the exchange'.

lessons.text: A piece that is attacked is not always free. Before you capture, look at what can take back.

quiz.q: White's knight attacks the pawn on e5. Should White play Nxe5?
options: No, the knight on c6 takes back
quiz.why: After Nxe5 Nxe5 White has given a knight (3) for a pawn (1). The pawn was attacked once and defended once, so it was safe.

lessons.text: Your opponent has just played ...Qh4, attacking your e4 pawn. Before you defend, run the check: is the piece that just moved safe on its new square?

move.prompt: Black's queen moved to a square you attack. Take it.
move.done: A whole queen. Always look at the piece that just moved: is it defended on its new square?

lessons.text: When several pieces aim at one square, count. If you attack a pawn more times than it is defended, you can win it. Here the d5 pawn is attacked twice (bishop and knight) and defended once (knight).

move.prompt: Win the pawn on d5.
move.done: Two attackers beat one defender. After the trades you are a pawn ahead.

lessons.text: The last step before you let go of a piece: imagine your move is played, then look at your opponent's checks, captures and threats. White would love to play Rd7 here, attacking f7.

quiz.q: Is Rd7 safe?
options: No, it allows ...Ra1+ and mate on the back rank
quiz.why: After Rd7?? Ra1+ White can only block with Rd1, and ...Rxd1 is checkmate. A quiet move like h3 first gives the king an escape square; then Rd7 is strong.

lessons.text: Put it together. Before every move: 1) What did their last move threaten? 2) Is my piece safe on the square it is going to? 3) What am I no longer defending when this piece moves?

quiz.q: You move a knight that was guarding your queen. Which question catches that mistake?
options: Is my piece safe on its new square?
What am I no longer defending?
quiz.why: Every piece that moves stops guarding something. Asking 'what did this piece defend?' catches a huge share of blunders.

courses.title: How to evaluate a position
courses.desc: Who is better, and why? Learn the five things to compare: material, king safety, piece activity, pawn structure and space.

lessons.text: When there is no tactic, you need a plan, and a plan starts with an evaluation. Compare the two sides on five points: material, king safety, piece activity, pawn structure and space.

quiz.q: In this symmetrical position, how would you judge it?
quiz.why: Both sides have the same material, safe kings, the same pawn structure and similar development. The position is about equal, with White's extra move a small plus.

lessons.text: Count material first: it is the easiest to measure. Pawn 1, knight and bishop 3, rook 5, queen 9. A lead of a full piece is normally enough to win.

quiz.q: Who is ahead on material?
quiz.why: White has two knights against one. With an extra piece the simplest plan is to trade pieces (not pawns) and win the endgame.

lessons.text: Material is not everything. A king with no pawns in front of it can be attacked along open lines, and an attack on the king can be worth more than a piece.

quiz.q: Material is equal here. Whose king is safer?
quiz.why: White's king sits behind three unmoved pawns. Black's g- and h-pawns are gone, so the g- and h-files and the light squares around the king are open. White should aim the queen and rooks at that side.

lessons.text: An active piece attacks things and has many squares. A passive piece only defends. Equal material with more active pieces is an advantage.

quiz.q: Whose rook is more active?
quiz.why: White's rook on the seventh rank attacks f7 and ties the black rook to defending a6. Black's rook cannot move without losing a pawn.

lessons.text: Pawns cannot move backwards, so weaknesses in the pawn structure last. A group of pawns on neighbouring files is a 'pawn island'. Fewer islands means the pawns can defend each other.

quiz.q: How many pawn islands does White have?
quiz.why: Four: a2, c3, the pair on e3 and f2, and h2. Black has only two islands. In an endgame, Black's king would have more targets to attack.

lessons.text: Space is the territory behind your pawns. More space means more room for your pieces. When you have compared all five points, play on the side where you are better, and improve the point where you are worse.

quiz.q: You are better on the queenside but your king is slightly exposed. What is a sensible plan?
options: Fix the king's safety, then play on the queenside
quiz.why: Play where you are stronger, and repair your weakest point first if the opponent can use it. A plan is simply the evaluation turned into moves.

courses.title: Good and bad pieces
courses.desc: Why a knight on an outpost can be worth a rook, when a bishop is 'bad', and how to improve your worst piece.

lessons.text: A bishop only ever sees squares of one colour. If your own central pawns are fixed on that colour, they block it. That is a 'bad' bishop. A bishop whose pawns are on the other colour is 'good'.

quiz.q: White's pawns on d4 and e5 stand on dark squares. Is White's dark-squared bishop on d2 good or bad?
quiz.why: Bad: it is hemmed in by its own pawns on d4 and e5. Black's pawns on d5 and e6 are on light squares, so a black dark-squared bishop would be the good one here.

lessons.text: An outpost is a square in the enemy half that no enemy pawn can ever attack, ideally one that your own pawn protects. A knight on an outpost cannot be chased away.

quiz.q: Why is the knight on d5 so strong?
options: No black pawn can attack it, and e4 supports it
quiz.why: Black has no c-pawn, and the e-pawn has already passed d5. Only a piece could remove the knight, and Black's dark-squared bishop can never touch a light square like d5.

lessons.text: Black's pawn on d6 is backward and the square in front of it, d5, can never be attacked by a black pawn. That square is waiting for a knight.

move.prompt: Jump into the outpost.
move.done: From d5 the knight eyes c7, e7, b6 and f6, and no pawn can touch it.

lessons.text: Bishops love open positions with long clear diagonals. Knights love closed positions, where pawns are locked and the knight can hop over them to an outpost.

quiz.q: The centre here is locked by pawn chains. Which minor piece would you rather have?
quiz.why: With the pawns locked, a bishop bumps into walls while a knight jumps over them. In an open position with pawns on both wings, choose the bishop.

lessons.text: Two bishops together cover squares of both colours. In open positions the 'bishop pair' is worth about half a pawn more than bishop and knight, or two knights.

quiz.q: You have the bishop pair. What kind of position should you aim for?
options: Open, with pawns traded in the centre
quiz.why: Open the position. Every pawn trade gives the bishops longer diagonals. If you are playing against the bishops, keep it closed.

lessons.text: When you cannot find a plan, ask: which of my pieces is doing the least? Then find a better square for it. Repeat. This simple rule produces good moves in almost any quiet position.

quiz.q: Which white piece most needs a better square?
quiz.why: The bishop on d2 is blocked by the pawn on e3. Opening the centre with e3-e4 at the right moment would give it a diagonal and bring it to life.

courses.title: Rooks: open files and the seventh rank
courses.desc: Rooks need open lines. Learn where they belong, why the seventh rank is so strong, and how to avoid back-rank disasters.

lessons.text: A rook behind its own pawn sees nothing. An open file, one with no pawns on it, is a road into the enemy position. Here the d-file and e-file are open.

move.prompt: Put a rook on an open file.
move.done: Now the rook controls the whole file and can enter Black's position.

lessons.text: If both sides want the same open file, the side with more rooks on it wins the fight. Two rooks on one file, one behind the other, are 'doubled'.

quiz.q: Both sides have a rook on the d-file, but White's rooks are doubled. Who controls the file right now?
quiz.why: Two rooks beat one. If Black trades with ...Rxd2, White takes back with the other rook and still holds the file. Black must bring the second rook to d8 to fight for it.

lessons.text: The best use of an open file is to reach the seventh rank. There the rook attacks the pawns that have not moved and keeps the enemy king on the back rank.

move.prompt: Send your rook to the seventh rank.
move.done: The rook attacks c7, and Black's rook must go passive to defend. A rook on the seventh is often worth a pawn.

lessons.text: Dr Tarrasch's rule: rooks belong behind passed pawns, your own or your opponent's. Behind your own pawn, the rook gains squares every time the pawn advances.

quiz.q: White's rook stands behind the a-pawn. What happens to the rook as the pawn moves up the board?
options: It gets more and more room
It gets less and less room
quiz.why: Each pawn step gives the rook another square behind it. A rook in front of its own pawn has the opposite problem: it gets in the way.

lessons.text: A castled king behind three unmoved pawns can be mated on the back rank by a rook or queen. One quiet pawn move, usually h3 or g3, gives the king an escape square. Players call it 'luft', German for air.

quiz.q: Black has already made luft with ...h6. Which quiet move does the same job for White?
quiz.why: After h3 the king can step to h2 if a rook checks on the back rank. Make luft when you have a spare move, before you need it.

lessons.text: To sum up: put rooks on open files, double them, aim for the seventh rank, keep them behind passed pawns, and make luft for your king.

quiz.q: There is no open file yet. Where should your rooks go?
options: Behind the pawns you plan to trade, so a file opens for them
quiz.why: Rooks should stand on files that are open or about to open. Plan a pawn trade, put a rook behind it, and the file is yours when it opens.

courses.title: Pawn weaknesses: isolated, doubled and backward
courses.desc: Learn to recognise the three weak pawns, why they are weak, and how to attack them.

lessons.text: Pawns are strongest side by side, where they protect each other. An isolated pawn has no friendly pawn on the files next to it, so only pieces can defend it.

quiz.q: Which black pawn is isolated?
quiz.why: Black has no c-pawn and no e-pawn, so nothing can ever protect d5 with a pawn. The square in front of it, d4, is also a perfect home for a white piece.

lessons.text: Doubled pawns are two pawns of the same colour on one file. They cannot protect each other, and the front one blocks the back one.

quiz.q: On which file does Black have doubled pawns?
quiz.why: Two black pawns stand on c6 and c5. They are not always bad (they can control useful squares), but in an endgame they are usually a weakness.

lessons.text: A backward pawn has fallen behind its neighbours and cannot safely advance, because the square in front of it is controlled by enemy pawns. It stays a target on a half-open file.

quiz.q: Which black pawn is backward?
quiz.why: The neighbours on c5 and e5 have moved ahead, and if the d-pawn steps to d5 it is captured by c4 or e4. The square d5 in front of it is an outpost for White.

lessons.text: The first step against an isolated pawn: stop it moving. Put a piece on the square directly in front of it. A knight is the best blockader, because it still attacks from there.

move.prompt: Blockade the d5 pawn with your knight.
move.done: The pawn is fixed. Because no black pawn can attack d4, the knight can stay there for the rest of the game.

lessons.text: Once the pawn is fixed, attack it with more pieces than can defend it. Every piece your opponent uses to guard a weak pawn is a piece that is not doing anything else.

quiz.q: White's rook attacks d5 through the knight. What is the idea of moving the knight away later, for example to b5 or f5?
options: To uncover the rook's attack on d5
quiz.why: When the knight steps aside, the rook attacks the pawn directly. Blockade first, then pile up: that is the standard plan against an isolated pawn.

lessons.text: A quick way to compare two pawn structures is to count pawn islands. The side with fewer islands usually has the healthier structure.

quiz.q: White has four islands, Black has two. Who has the better structure?
quiz.why: Black. Two compact groups defend themselves; four scattered groups need pieces to guard them. When trading pieces, ask which side the pawn endgame would favour.

courses.title: Passed pawns
courses.desc: A passed pawn is a queen in waiting. Learn to spot one, push it, blockade it and create one with a breakthrough.

lessons.text: A passed pawn has no enemy pawn in front of it on its own file or on the two files beside it. No pawn can stop it, so pieces have to.

quiz.q: Which white pawn is passed?
quiz.why: Black has no pawn on the c-, d- or e-file, so nothing can block or capture the d-pawn on its way to d8.

lessons.text: Can a lone king catch a passed pawn? Draw a square from the pawn to its promotion square. If the king can step inside the square on its move, it catches the pawn. If not, the pawn promotes.

move.prompt: It is your move. The black king is one step too far away. Run!
move.done: The king was outside the square, so the pawn became a queen without any help.

lessons.text: 'Passed pawns must be pushed', but the defender has an answer: put a piece on the square in front of the pawn. The best blockader is a knight, which is not bothered by standing still.

quiz.q: On which square should Black's knight blockade this pawn?
quiz.why: The square directly in front, d6. Blockade the pawn early, before it gets far: the closer it comes to promotion, the more of your pieces it ties down.

lessons.text: A passed pawn that is defended by another pawn is a 'protected passed pawn'. The enemy king cannot simply walk up and capture it.

quiz.q: Why can the black king never capture the pawn on d5 while the c4 pawn stays?
quiz.why: The pawn on c4 protects d5. In king and pawn endgames a protected passed pawn is often decisive, because the enemy king can never leave it.

lessons.text: An 'outside' passed pawn is far away from the other pawns. The enemy king must walk all the way over to stop it, and that leaves the other side of the board unprotected.

quiz.q: Black's king goes to stop the a-pawn. What does White's king do meanwhile?
options: Attacks the black pawns on the kingside
quiz.why: The a-pawn is a decoy. While Black's king is busy on the a-file, White's king walks in and wins the f- and g-pawns.

lessons.text: Sometimes you must sacrifice pawns to make a passed pawn. This is the most famous example: three pawns against three, and White to move wins.

move.prompt: Start the breakthrough with the middle pawn.
move.done: Two pawns given, and the a-pawn cannot be stopped. (If Black takes the other way, ...cxb6, then a6! does the same job.)

courses.title: Checkmate patterns every player must know
courses.desc: Eight classic mating patterns. Learn the shape once and you will spot it in your own games.

lessons.text: The king is trapped on the back rank by its own pawns. A rook or queen arriving on that rank gives mate.

move.prompt: Deliver the back-rank mate.
move.done: The pawns on f7, g7 and h7 blocked every escape square.

lessons.text: The queen gives check right next to the enemy king, protected by one of your own pieces, so the king cannot take her.

move.prompt: Give mate with the queen, protected by your king.
move.done: The queen covers every square around the king, and your own king protects her.

lessons.text: The fastest checkmate in chess. White has pushed the f- and g-pawns and opened the diagonal to the king.

move.prompt: You are Black. Punish it.
move.done: Mate in two moves. Lesson: be very careful about moving the pawns in front of your king.

lessons.text: Queen and bishop both attack f7, the weakest square in Black's camp because only the king defends it. Black has just played ...Nf6 and missed the threat.

move.prompt: Finish the game on f7.
move.done: The bishop protects the queen, so the king cannot capture her. Now you know how to stop it: defend f7 or block with ...g6.

lessons.text: Two rooks (or queen and rook) take turns: one guards a rank so the king cannot step forward, the other gives check on the next one.

move.prompt: One rook holds the seventh rank. Give mate with the other.
move.done: The rook on a7 guards the seventh rank; the rook on b8 covers the eighth.

lessons.text: The king is surrounded by its own pieces and has no square at all. Only a knight can give check in such a position, and that check is mate.

move.prompt: Give the smothered mate.
move.done: The king is 'smothered' by its own rook and pawns.

lessons.text: One of the oldest patterns in chess: rook and knight against a king in the corner. The knight protects the rook and takes away the last escape square.

move.prompt: Give mate with the rook.
move.done: The knight on f6 guards both the rook and the square g8.

lessons.text: Queen in front, bishop behind on the same diagonal, both aiming at h7. With no knight on f6 to defend, the queen lands with mate.

move.prompt: Capture on h7 with the queen.
move.done: The bishop protects the queen on h7, and the rook on f8 blocks the king's escape. A knight on f6 would have stopped this, which is why it is such an important defender.

courses.title: Endgame principles
courses.desc: The ideas behind every endgame: the active king, the opposition, the rule of the square and when to trade.

lessons.t: The king is a fighting piece
lessons.text: In the middlegame the king hides. In the endgame, with the queens gone, it becomes a strong piece worth about four points. The first job in most endgames is to bring the king to the centre.

quiz.q: Where should White's king head?
options: Towards the centre, for example e3 and d4
quiz.why: A centralised king can go to either wing and attacks enemy pawns. The side whose king arrives first usually wins a pawn ending.

lessons.text: When two kings face each other with one square between them, neither can step forward. The player who does NOT have to move 'has the opposition': the other king must give way.

quiz.q: It is White's move here. Who has the opposition?
quiz.why: Black. White has to move, so White's king must step aside or back, and Black's king can advance. If it were Black's move, White would have the opposition.

lessons.text: With king and pawn against king, the attacker wants the king in front of the pawn with the opposition. One king move here takes it; the other natural move lets Black take it and draw.

move.prompt: Step forward so the kings face each other with one square between them.
move.done: Kings on d5 and d7 with Black to move: you have the opposition. Black's king must give way and your king will escort the pawn. After the tempting Ke5? Ke7! Black would have had it, and the game is a draw.

lessons.text: To see whether a king catches a passed pawn, picture a square whose side runs from the pawn to its promotion square. Here that square has corners a5, a8, d8 and d5. If the king can step into it, the king is in time.

quiz.q: It is Black's move, with the king on d1. Can Black catch the pawn?
options: No, the king is too far away
quiz.why: The square reaches down only to the fifth rank. A king on d1 needs four moves to reach it; it is hopelessly outside, and the pawn promotes.

lessons.text: When you are ahead on material, every trade of pieces makes your extra piece matter more. But keep pawns on the board: you need them to make a queen. The side that is behind wants the opposite.

quiz.q: White is a knight up. Which trades should White welcome?
quiz.why: Trade pieces and keep pawns. A lone knight cannot mate, so White must keep pawns to promote. The defender tries to trade off all the pawns.

lessons.text: In rook endgames, the commonest endgames of all, the rook belongs behind the passed pawn, where it supports every step. And an active rook is worth more than a pawn: do not go passive to defend one.

quiz.q: Where does a rook stand best in relation to a passed pawn?
quiz.why: Behind it, whether the pawn is yours or the opponent's. You can practise the two key rook endings, Lucena and Philidor, in the Endgame trainer.
